title: A friend has repeated something you told them in confidence
lede: Something private is now in general circulation, and the trail runs back to the one person you told. They have not admitted it and possibly do not know that you know.

blocks.text: Something private is now in general circulation, and the trail runs back to the one person you told. They have not admitted it and possibly do not know that you know.

items: Most confidence breaches are carelessness rather than malice — told to one person as gossip currency, then travelled. This matters because malice and carelessness need different responses.
The damage is already done. The only live question is what your relationship becomes now.
Confronting on secondhand information is risky. Confirm the chain before you spend the friendship on it.
The temptation to punish by withdrawal — going cold without explanation — feels safe and destroys more than the original leak.

items.detail: Who said it, who did they hear it from, how specific was it. One wrong accusation costs you both the friend and the moral position.
If the information can still cause practical harm — job, relationship, health — deal with the harm before the friendship.

items.move: Have one conversation, in private, in person if possible
items.detail: Not in a group, not by message. Messages get screenshotted and forwarded, which is exactly how you got here.

items.move: Describe the impact rather than the crime
items.detail: People defend against accusations and respond to impact. This is the difference between a repair and a war.

items.move: Ask a direct question and then be quiet
items.detail: Let them answer without help. Their first response tells you almost everything.
Full repair, reduced trust, or ending it. All three are legitimate; drifting is not.

items.say: "I need to ask you something directly. Did you tell anyone about the thing I told you in March?"
"Three people have mentioned it to me. I felt exposed at work and I did not know it was coming."
"I believe you did not mean harm. It still landed on me, and I need to know it will not happen again."
"I want to stay friends. I am not going to tell you the serious things for a while, and I would rather say that than pretend."

items: Retaliating with something of theirs. It ends any chance that you are the reasonable party.
Broadcasting the betrayal to the shared group. It forces everyone to choose and usually costs you more of them than it costs them.
Demanding they identify everyone they told and retract it. It cannot be done and it makes you look controlling.
Pretending it did not happen while quietly punishing them for a year.
Assume the information is permanent and plan around it existing, not around it being recalled.
Notice the pattern: was this the first time? If it is the third, the problem is your disclosure policy, not their character.
Rebuild in small increments if you choose repair. Trust is restored by low-stakes reliability, not by one big conversation.
Write down, for yourself, the two or three people who have never once leaked. That is your actual inner circle.

limit: If the betrayal involved your money, your login credentials, your professional reputation, or intimate images, treat it as a security and legal matter alongside a personal one. Change credentials, preserve the evidence with dates, and get advice before you confront them — confrontation destroys evidence.
